utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I have heard nothing about preliminaries. For the Prosecution, who is going to deal with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Adam Weber on behalf of the Prosecution. At this time the Prosecution would seek leave to present the evidence of John Hamill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Mr. Hamill.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Hamill.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, you'll first be examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find him to your right. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your full name along with your current rank and assignment in the Irish defence forces.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: My name is John Gerard Brendan Hamill. I'm a lieutenant-colonel in the Irish defence forces, and I am currently serving in defence force headquarters in Dublin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you provided evidence before this Tribunal on three previous occasions in the cases of Prosecutor versus Galic, Prosecutor versus Kordic and Cerkez, and most recently in the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to review your previous testimony in the Galic case prior to today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are there any corrections that you would like to make to this previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No. That testimony stands as given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions that you were asked in the Galic case would your answers be the same, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution tenders a redacted version of Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill's previous testimony in Galic as a public exhibit. The transcript has been uploaded under 65 ter 28551.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It becomes Exhibit P537, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P537 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During your previous testimony in Galic, you commented upon the UNPROFOR investigation report dated 15 February 1994, which related to your investigation into the shelling of the Markale market on 5 February 1994. Did you again review this report and its annexes prior to your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were there duplicates of a report by a Captain Verdy and cover pages included in these materials?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: There were. There were three copies of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders two exhibits associated to the witness's previous testimony. The Prosecution has removed the duplicates and cover pages from 65 ter 10010 and tenders the materials uploaded under 65 ter 10010A. The second 65 ter number is 17881, which is a map marked by the witness during the previous testimony. The Prosecution tenders both exhibits publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence as to either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 10010A receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P538, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P538 is admitted into evidence. 65 ter 17881, map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P539, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P539 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours with your leave the Prosecution would request permission to present the public summary of Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel John Hamill served in Sarajevo as a United Nations military observer from May to August 1993. During this period, he worked exclusively in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or SRK-held territory. His duties and functions at the time included monitoring the use of weapons as well as carrying out a liaison function at the SRK command in Lukavica. In February 1994, Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill returned to Sarajevo as a technical advisor to a United Nations team tasked with investigating the shelling of the Markale market. During the course of the team's investigations, the witness had occasion to speak with the Bosnian Serb Army's designated liaison for the team, a Colonel Cvetkovic, whom he understood to be the commander of a SRK artillery regiment. In the course of this interview, Colonel Cvetkovic confirmed there were a number of 120-millimetre mortars to the north-north-east of the Markale market in Mrkovici, and he said that in the previous year, the BSA artillery had fired 30.000 to 40.000 rounds into the city. He asked Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill why they were so concerned about the one round when they had fired so many. Although not personally present at his UNMO position on 1 June 1993, this witness examined two shell craters in Dobrinja in 2001 related to scheduled incident G4. This concludes the summary of the witness, Your Honours, may I proceed with my questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 6163 of your previous testimony, you stated: "I certainly remember times when 3.600 rounds were fired into the city from the north over a 12-hour period." Who would fire the large quantity of rounds on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Those rounds would have been fired by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps artillery, which was based in the area north of Vogosca and Radava, north of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution sought leave to add three exhibits for this witness. At this time, I would seek permission to use one of those three exhibits. It has been uploaded as 65 ter 28554. It is an UNMO sitrep related to the time period Mr. Hamill was present in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 28554 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the Sector Sarajevo UNMO daily sitrep for 21 and 22 July 1993, which is now before you, do you recall the shelling described in the "General situation" section of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what happened on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: At that time most of the area north of Sarajevo was closed to the military observers from the United Nations organisation. However, we were still able to listen to and hear shelling going on from the area east of Rajlovac, in other words, Vogosca, Radava, Polinje, and we heard and recorded a total as you see here of 3.777 rounds which impacted in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on your experience as an artillery officer, what level of command could have authorised such an expenditure of artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: This was a very high-level --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object that they're asking for an expert opinion, they're asking for a conclusion, and they're asking for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it's all of the three, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question as phrased is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill, in your previous testimony it is indicated that you had been an artillery officer since 1974, and you also discuss your experience with the command staff of the SRK. Based on your experience with artillery and also your familiarity with the SRK command staff in Lukavica, are you able to comment at all on what level of command could have authorised such an expenditure of artillery on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking the same, Mr. Weber, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I'm happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could I please have the top of page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under the section entitled "Restrictions to UNMO movement," the sitrep states: "Patrolling of the Lima 11 area is still impossible by the local and armed gang leader." Do you know who is the local and armed gang leader being referred to in the sitrep?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do. His name was Vasilije Vidovic and I had personal experience of him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On pages 6063 and 6218 to 6219 of your previous testimony you discuss Vidovic and his men. You stated on page 6218 that you believed these men were under the control of a particular officer. What was the name of this officer in?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I was informed that they were under the command of a General Josipovic, who apparently was in charge of most of the northern Sarajevo Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28554 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It becomes Exhibit P540, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P540 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 13707.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the sector Sarajevo UNMO daily sitrep for 23 and 24 July 1993 which is now before you, are you familiar with the "General situation" section of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know if the situation described in this sitrep was part of the same events that we just saw from a few days earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is my belief that it is, because it was just two days after the previous events, and it would appear to be just a continuation of the same operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 13707 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It becomes Exhibit P541, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P541 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 19268. Your Honours, just to inform the Court, the translation is still pending for this, but we do expect this shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no idea yet what it is, so it's -- let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill, the Prosecution would like to go through some available information from the 18 hours prior to the shelling of the Markale market on 5 February, 1994. Do you recognise the type of document that is now before you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What kind of document is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: This was a CapSat transmission, an update to the daily situation report of the UNMOs in Sarajevo, and it was given at midnight on the 4th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does this update relate to a particular time period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It relates to the period from 1800 hours to midnight on the 4th of February, the day before the Markale incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What do the four-digit numbers that appear within the parentheses represent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The four-digit numbers are grid references each covering a kilometre square.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This update refers to BiH in as 64 mixed and 14 AAA, no BiH outgoing were heard or seen. It reflects eight mixed and 50 AAA outgoing from the BSA. What does it mean when an UNMO reports either impacts or outgoing fire as mixed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Mixed would mean a combination of guns and mortars. It's not always possible to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- if I may, I would object to the question as phrased insofar as it appears the counsel is now testifying. Unless the witness has some personal knowledge of this or can confirm having been receiving this document, I don't believe that the material in the document can be submitted in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see. What now exactly -- "It reflects eight mixed and 50 AAA outgoing from...," is that what you're referring to, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We've established the date of this is February 5th 1994, at a time period when this witness was not in Sarajevo as part of the UNMO mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. But, Mr. Weber, could you ask the witness when he was -- when he took up office and when he left it, whether there was a standard system of referring to issues like mixed or AAA so that we know what the basis of his knowledge is when he answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill, was there a standard system of referring to issues like mixed or AAA that UNMOs used when reporting either outgoing or incoming fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I had spent nearly nine months in the operation at that time, part of the time writing these reports, part of the time receiving the reports at the headquarters in Zagreb. And if possible, one should distinguish between tank, mortar, and artillery fire, but it wasn't always possible. So they would be referred to as mixed. But if at all possible, the items, the explosions, should be separated out into what type of weapon fired them. AAA refers to anti-aircraft artillery fire. The mixed would refer to a possible combination of tank rounds, gun rounds, or mortar rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of this 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill, this is an UNMO daily sitrep for Sector Sarajevo for 5 February 1994, between the hours of 0001 and 0800. Could you please review this document and let us know when you've completed it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you aware of these last two sitreps when you conducted your investigation into the Markale shelling in February 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I don't believe that I was, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The sitrep before you indicates that residential areas in the city centre were shelled. What is the objective of shelling residential areas between these hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, would you rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on your own military experience, is there any legitimate military purpose to targeting residential areas between these hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object. Calls for legal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if you ask the witness perhaps about what he learned during his education about shelling during the day-time you might receive the information you're apparently seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill, throughout your experiences with the Irish Defence forces, have you ever receive training and also provided instruction on whether or not certain targets would be considered legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please briefly tell us what that experience is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: A legitimate target is a target which is of high value which is military and which is not one which would be against the Law of Armed Conflict, such as a city centre or a residential area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would you consider the shelling the city centre between the hours of midnight and 8.00 that's reflected in this sitrep before you to be a legitimate military activity based your experience and training?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, same objection, same legal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, these kind of conclusions, Mr. Weber, of course are for the Chamber. The Chamber might be assisted by knowing what the effect of this type of shelling would be under those circumstances. So if you would wish to elicit such evidence, it is not covered by the objection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What would the effect of this type of shelling be under these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Unless there was a military target involved which was engaged in active military activity, I cannot conceive of any reason for shelling the area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 19268 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object insofar as the witness at transcript page 11, line 17, said he doesn't believe that he was provided these at the time that he was involved in the Markale investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ivetic, just one short question. Apparently Mr. Weber wants to establish what knowledge Mr. Hamill did not have at that time, and by showing him a document and saying, Did you have this knowledge available, would that not shed additional light on what knowledge the witness had at the time and what knowledge he did not have?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if the witness can add something to the document it could be admitted through the witness otherwise it's not for this witness who has neither authored the document nor received the document, nor is it during the time period that he had personal knowledge of the events in question since he was not in Sarajevo after August of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies the objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 19268 becomes Exhibit P542, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P542 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could please leave it MFI'd, I'm sorry, just pending the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has to be MFI'd. Sorry for that mistake. And there's another matter. Mr. Ivetic, you have not asked it to be read so that it could be translated for Mr. Mladic. May I take it that there was no need to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I correct my earlier pronunciation of admission and P542 is marked for identification waiting translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P538, page 42 of the English original only. The B/C/S translation is on page 55, but it is simply a duplicate of the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill, this is a document that was annexed to your 15 February 1994 UNPROFOR investigation report. Could you please tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: This document is an Increp or incident report from the Papa side, which is the Presidency side of the UNMO operation within Sarajevo. And what an incident report is is a report on the incoming shells and other types of munitions into the area of the Presidency side during the period in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What date does this Increp relate to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It relates to the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the far left column entitled "Sender serial," what do the letters and numbers in this column represent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The first two letters and numbers, the letter and the digit -- Papa 3, for example refers to an UNMO post known as Papa 3 on the Presidency side. As they logged the income shells, mortar shells, 4 mortar shells from 0530 to 0535, they gave it a serial number, 01. Similarly Papa 2 at 0645 logged one mortar bomb and gave it the title Papa 2-01 and so on down. So it relates to the UNMO post and the number that they had allocated to the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I know you've started to explain some of the other information in this document, but if I could direct you specifically to the centre column entitled "Activity details." There are letters followed by a number, and then separately a four-digit number. Could you please tell us what these notations represent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The letter refers to the type of weapon that is being used. So if memory serves me correctly, Alpha or A is for guns, B is for mortars, C is for tanks, and so on. The number immediately following the first letter refers to the number of rounds of that type of munition, and then the four digits at the right-hand side of that column refers to the grid reference, the 1 kilometre square within which the munitions fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I know you've started to explain it, but just so we have a clear record, on the basis of the explanations you just provided, would it be correct to interpret the first entry, as an example, as indicating there were four mortar impacts observed by a Papa team between 5.30 and 5.35 in the morning in grid 9259?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That's precisely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this page there's an entry for Markale. Do you have any observations of the shelling activity leading up to this entry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: This entry is -- is quite specific. It says that Markale is in grid 9260, which is incorrect. It's actually in grid 9259. But going to the substance of your question, it shows that there were mortar bombs falling within the Sarajevo city centre area in the period leading up to that particular one bomb on Markale, some at 10.00 in grids 9059 and some reported by Papa 5 between 11.30 and 12.45 in grid 9159, which is the neighbouring grid to the Markale grid. It's approximately anything from 900 to 1.900 metres from Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please have the lower part of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have any observations of the shelling activity after the Markale entry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Clearly shelling continued throughout the day from mortars, from tanks, and fell generally in the city centre and also in the western part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Overall, how would you describe the level of activity on the -- on 5 February 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It wasn't very heavy. It was relatively light. It was a normal Sarajevo day, from my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've mentioned that the grid reference of 9260 for Markale was incorrect. Did you have the opportunity during proofing yesterday to compare this reference to a map and also the six-digit grid reference of 929596 listed on the first page of these investigative materials?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please briefly explain the difference between a four-digit and a six-digit grid reference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I think the Chamber received evidence that a three-digit grid reference gives a square of 1 kilometre by 1 kilometre, whereas a four-digit gives a square of 100 metres by 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's almost correct, Your Honour. Almost correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Almost correct. Then, please, it's always good to know where our understanding is wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's --a four-digit grid gives one square kilometre and a six-digit grid is 100 metres by 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what I meant to say, as a matter of fact, is that four is 2 by 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Six is 3 by 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3 by 3, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, yes, now I think we understood this estimate. Thank you. Please proceed Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 9821A for the witness. It is a map. There's no translation. If we could please have it magnified in the upper right-hand corner of this map. If we could please have an additional magnification. Could the witness please be provided with a pen. I believe the witness has one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you need a special pen, Mr. Hamill, to mark anything on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I imagine this is possibly it. It was connected to the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we have different colours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill, are you able to locate the grid references on the map before you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please locate the spot associated to the six-digit grid reference of 929596 on the map before you and circle it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please place an X inside of the area corresponding to grid 9260.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders this map as marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked version of 65 ter 9821A becomes Exhibit P543, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has no further questions at this time. We tender the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, you'll now be cross examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. You will find him to your left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill. Before I begin with my questions, I'd like to take the chance to remind you that since we both speak English, we have to be mindful to have pauses between question and answer so that the translator and -- the translators and the court reporter can keep up with us. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And let's begin with the questions. First of all, sir, could you please tell us what, if any, training or instruction specific to the constitutional framework of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia you received prior to your deployment to Bosnia as part of the UN?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In terms of formal training, I can say that I received none specifically, except that I educated myself by reading what I could not on the constitution but on the history of former Yugoslavia as it was and also of the conflict to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you undergo or undertake any special review or training or instruction as to the armed forces and/or the defence system of the former Yugoslavia such as the structure of the JNA, the structure of the VRS, or the structure of the so-called Armija BiH?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that instruction entailed? Was it -- first of all, was it self-education?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, it was provided by my defence forces at home prior to my deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How extensive was it in terms of the amount of time that was spent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Extensive enough that as a trained military officer with more than 20 years' experience, I was well able to take in what a normal military structure was and is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For those of us without 20 years' experience, how long is it in terms of hours, days, weeks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I had 20 years' experience on training of being a military officer. I was a senior officer at the time. I completed a command and staff course with distinction. I had degree, and I had post-graduate training. So I can't actually quantify how much training I received during my military experience which would enable me to understand foreign armies, but take it that it was something in the region of two full years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there maybe some confusion. I think that you are interested to know what specific additional training the witness received shortly before he went to the former Yugoslavia, perhaps after he had heard that he would be sent there. Is that -- could you tell us how intensive or how much time briefing and instructions took once you knew that you would be sent to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I cannot recall specifically at this time, but it was certainly a period of a number of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That answers the question, I take it, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you were first deployed to Bosnia-Herzegovina were you able to speak the local language, or did you have to rely upon an interpret?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I relied upon interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were the interpreters that were used locals, that is to say locals from Yugoslavia, or were they persons that came from outside of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: They were all Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to use the same interpreters when you were part of the UNMO mission as you used when you did your subsequent investigations into the Markale and the Dobrinja incidents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No. I used interpreters which were employed by UNMO Sarajevo during my deployment there. When I went back subsequently I used interpreters which were employed by the ICTY, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's break that up. You say you used interpreters by the ICTY. Are you referring there to the Dobrinja investigation but not the Markale, I would imagine?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not the Markale, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to any briefings that you received as part of the UNMO mission, am I correct that you were -- part of your briefings entailed a warning that the Bosnian Presidency forces in town could very well place dead bodies in crime scenes to create a false image?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: This was stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to confirm some things about the skills or science involved in the use of artillery. In order to assist us, I would like to turn to some of your testimony in the Kordic and Cerkez case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if we can call up document 1D438 in e-court. And if we could turn to the second page of that document. I believe it will be transcript page 16184. And if we can focus on the fifth and sixth line onward. It would be lines 5 through 19, approximately, that I'd like to draw the witness's attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, here I will present to you the portion of the transcript beginning the end of line 5 through line 19 and ask you to comment on it afterwards: "Q. One point of amplification: Is calculating the place from which artillery fires a practical skill used by soldiers on the ground? "A. Yes, it is. "Q. The reason being, that if you are being fired at, and you can't see where the guns are firing from, you actually need to work it out? "A. You need to work it out in order to return fire. "Q. Is that a skill, therefore, in which artillery officers are trained? "A. Yes. "Q. And were you so trained? "A. I was." First of all, sir, as a formality can you confirm the selection of the transcript I have read as being true and accurate in form?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I presume it is. I haven't seen it in the past 12 years or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that in this case, that is to say the Kordic case, you were testifying as an expert having performed approximately one week of an analysis of a particular shelling in the city of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when it's recorded here that you said if one doesn't see the artillery firing you have to "work it out in order to return fire," could you tell us, does this mean that one must examine the crater hits from incoming fire to determine the potential source?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is one method. There are other methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Using any of these methods is this an instantaneous process or does it take time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Using that process, it takes time. And furthermore, it is only possible to get the general direction from which the weapon was fired. It is not possible to calculate the range.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the case of mortars that are used in a shoot and scoot manner by the other side, is it fairly possible that the weapons that were the source of incoming fire can be long gone by the time that the receiving side works out the direction where from the fire came and attempts to return fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe to us what is shoot and scoot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Shoot and scoot is used by mortars, because mortar fire is easily detected, mortars are slow weapons, the -- the projectile is subsonic, so it can be detected in the air by a missile system, for example, which would then give the operator of the missile system -- or sorry, the radar system a means of locating where the mortar was firing from. So mortar will go into a position. It will fire a number of rounds, and it will then leave. So it shoots and it scoots. It leaves the area and redeploys elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that this shoot and scoot is a mortar tactic that is taught and used by NATO-aligned forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this was a tactic, shoot and scoot, which was taught under the SFRY or JNA system?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I would imagine that it was, but it was not the way that mortars were deployed in Sarajevo by the SRK. It was used by the Presidency side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for the sake of clarity, I believe you may have already touched upon this topic, but the process of working out the source of incoming fire can only determine the bearing, because the range of the incoming shell is determined on the amount of charge that is placed on the mortar round; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I also correct that there is no forensic evidence that can be obtained at the site of a round impact as to the amount of charge that was on that round because all of this was used up at the time of firing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That's precisely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I apologise, this may seem like a layman's question, it may be foolish to you, but is it possible to determine how far a shot has travelled in relation to how far -- how deep it has impacted on a hard surface, that is to say the funnel -- the fuse tunnel or furrow of the crater?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I am not aware of any publication which would give that type of information. Particularly as when the round impacts on the ground, the surface can be of various different types. It can be concrete which is reinforced, concrete which is not reinforced. There can be asphalt. There can be earth. You know, it's just simply not possible to establish how -- how far it had come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you earlier had problems with expert matters. It is my recollection reading some of the judgement of this Tribunal that the matters you are addressing at this moment were dealt with by experts extremely specialised in this area, including the issues as you just mentioned them. Therefore, I'm wondering whether or not the basis of the knowledge of this witness on these matters should be tested before we ask questions around these matters, apart from whether this is expert evidence or not. I am perhaps a bit little less concerned by it in the formal sense than you are. The same may be true for my colleagues. But is there anyway, for example, to ask the witness whether he's aware of studies of the composition of the ground in relation to the penetration of the sound by projectiles, whether he has any knowledge of that? Mr. Hamill, perhaps -- I think you heard the question. Are you aware of any studies of impact -- of projectiles on the various types of soil, concrete? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen such literature, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the matter of the expertise arises here, Mr. Ivetic, and I'm quite willing -- perhaps we should not discuss it in the presence of the witness. Therefore, I suggest that we take a break in a couple of minutes but that we already invite the witness to leave the courtroom and take the break -- before we take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you would read the proceedings, for example, in the Galic case, you'd find out that - and, of course, I'm referring to that case only - that experts of the Prosecution, expert of the Defence, both trained in the same field - I think even one being the professor of the other - agreed on important matters which required a thorough knowledge of exactly the kind of things Mr. Hamill has just told us he doesn't know about. So therefore, I wonder what is the use of asking these questions which require not only a bit of expertise but the highest possible expertise, which was, as I understand, only developed in the cases before this Tribunal, and then to ask the witness questions in the area where he has clearly shown to have no knowledge, let alone expert knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, then I'm really confused, because the basis and bulk of this witness's testimony in direct examination were two analyses that he performed of incoming fire, one for the Prosecution, one for the United Nations, and which are the bulk of his testimony. So is he or is he not qualified to talk about examination of craters which is precisely the area that I'm asking him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say -- I'm inclined to say that with the limited training and therefore also with the limited results, if I ask someone who is not very trained in a certain area, I should explore the level of his training, and whatever his conclusions are is always limited by the level of his knowledge. If that is -- if you would agree with that and that whatever the witness says, and when you're talking about the range of fire whether you could draw any conclusions on the basis of the composition of the soil, if the witness says, I do not know, apparently he's not familiar with that subject. And, therefore, if he would draw conclusions for which you would need to know that and that would, for example, not be crater analysis which does not pay attention to the depth of impact but just pays attention to the origin of fire in a more broad sense, that it came approximately from this direction without saying anything to the range, as the witness said, then I think we would -- we would be assisted by this evidence, also by knowing what its limited meaning has to be. Would you -- is this something you would agree to or not, because then we can leave out the composition and depth of impact if it comes to any further details which would lead to assessing the range of fire other than in terms of direction, at least on the basis of the composition of the soil. I see you're nodding yes, which doesn't appear on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will be happy to ask him as to his experiences of doing crater analyses and the education and training he has had in that regard if that will assists in terms of his knowledge base for the answers to the questions he provided to the Prosecution and to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Weber, would you agree with this approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break, and we resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber establishes that the accused, that Mr. Mladic, is not in the courtroom. Could you provide us any further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. After the end of the first session, Mr. Mladic complained that he was not feeling well, that he's dizzy, and in the room we were in, a medical worker took his pressure, and his pressure is close to the maximum normal. He says he feels his right-hand side of the body is feeling numb. It was said that medics from the Detention Unit will be consulted, and we asked what was going to happen afterwards. We also asked Mr. Mladic if he was able to join us in the courtroom. He said he was not, and he asked us to inform you thereof, and he also asked to be given the necessary assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we do understand that Mr. Mladic receives the assistance he has asked for. He says he is unable to join and to inform us about that. Can we continue as far as the Defence is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he did not authorise us to continue without his presence while he is in such a condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean -- of course, the Chamber decides on whether or not there are sufficient reasons not to proceed. Would that mean that if we decide to proceed that you would not further cross-examine the witness? Is that -- or Mr. Ivetic would not further examine the witness? Is that -- because I'm not telling you a secret when I say that we had a long history of claims about not feeling well which finally were medically not substantiated. That is the reason why the Chamber is a bit cautious in not proceeding. The Chamber is also aware that if we would proceed, first of all that everything is audio and video recorded. Second, that if the appropriate remedy would be to hear again part of the testimony of the witness that that is still an option to be considered, but we have lost considerable time for claims of feeling unable to attend where there was no medical basis for that. Therefore, the question is: What if the Chamber now would decide to proceed, again with all the caveats I just gave to you, possibility to follow the proceedings? We'll know soon whether there are any medical reasons for Mr. Mladic, that he cannot attend as he claims until now. Would you like to briefly discuss this with Mr. Mladic? Then we would take a break of another -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Moloto has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the person who you say attended to Mr. Mladic was interpreted as a medical worker? What kind of medical worker is this? What's the qualification of the person?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we do not know that. I'm saying that no medical assistance has been given to Mr. Mladic, only his pressure was taken. That's all we were told about his pressure. And we were also told that Dr. Falke from the Detention Unit will be consulted immediately because of the indications presented by Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is: The medical worker who took his pressure, what level of qualification is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take -- we'll take a break of ten minutes. During these ten minutes, Mr. Stojanovic, you have an opportunity to further discuss the matter with Mr. Mladic, and the Chamber will have a possibility to further inquire into what has happened until now and what the exact situation is. We take a break and we resume at 20 minutes past 11.00. --- Break taken at 11.10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I establish that Mr. Mladic is present in the courtroom. Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber has used the break to consult Dr. Gerts, and the Chamber establishes that as matters stand now, on the basis of the information we have now, that there is no objective medical reason to support the absence of Mr. Mladic in court, and we would have proceeded without his presence if he would not have appeared in court. Second, the Chamber takes it that the time we've lost with all this should not make any change in this week's schedule. So therefore, keep this in the back of your mind that the last half hour is a half an hour you have lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a bit longer than you may have expected. Mr. Ivetic will now resume his cross-examination. Mr. Ivetic, the Judges briefly discussed the matter, and I think the preferred way of proceeding is to first ask what the witness did and found and only after that pay attention to whether that fits into his expertise or his special knowledge. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In terms of the crater analyses that you have performed in the course of your career, including the one at the Markale site and the Dobrinja site, am I correct that you estimate a range of possible distances that a round travelled based upon the type of shell and the known range table for that or similar type of ordnance based on the various possible charges that could be fitted to the same?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, how are these range tables generated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Range tables are generated by the manufacturers of the ammunition in co-operation with the manufacturers of the weapon. The range tables provide information in relation to the range depending on the number of charges that are fitted to the particular type of projectile and the angle at which it is fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in performing your crater analysis of these two sites and all of them that you have formed in your career, am I correct that depending on the number of charges that are fitted to a shell before it is fired the maximum distance of a particular ordnance could vary by as much as a few hundred metres to over several kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the analysis that you performed, am I correct that based upon the minimum and maximum ranges of a particular ordnance that you have found to have landed, you then look at known or fixed locations of artillery or mortars to determine what potential sources for that fire exist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not necessarily, because, of course, weapons can be moved from their positions and are regularly moved from their positions. That was not normally the case in the case of the RSK weaponry around Sarajevo. As I have previously indicated in previous evidence, it normally stayed in the same position. However, what one does find are general areas, six in this case, where the weapon could have fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to clarify, you said RSK. Did you mean SRK, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sorry, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the six locations that you said that the fire could have come from, were these all locations where there was existing artillery in place either on the Armija side or the SRK side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we're just causing possibly a little confusion in the record. There's been reference to multiple analyses and now there is discussion of six locations. Maybe for clarity we could establish which one of the investigations he's now discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have suggested, Mr. Ivetic, that the preferred way of proceeding is to find out what the witness did and what he observed, and to do that in general terms might be less assisting the Chamber than if you look at what did you do here, what did you do there? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I thought we were talking about Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: So did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With -- with regard to -- let's stick with Markale for the moment. In the case of a mobile mortar or one being used in a shoot and scoot capacity, would it be difficult to locate such pieces through any type of analysis that you do?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That's a very difficult question to answer. If there was a fixed position from which the mortar normally fired, then clearly it would be visible, but in the fact that because the possible positions cover a large area, it would be very difficult to find any physical evidence that the mortar had fired from there. We're talking in terms of an area possibly hundreds of metres long by tens and possibly a hundred metres wide. Because of the inherent inaccuracy of a mortar, we're looking backwards rather than forwards, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. If I can direct specifically to Markale, the areas that were the potential sources for fire that you say covered a larger area, is it possible for a mobile mortar being used in a shoot and scoot capacity to have been the origin of that shot and to therefore no longer be an identifiable mortar position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned the inherit inaccuracy of a mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask. You're asking a general question, but you say it is about Markale. That makes it a hypothetical question, I take it, that -- I'm a bit confused by this is Markale and then to ask potential sources of fire, larger area. Is it possible for a mobile mortar being used in that and that capacity. So you're subsuming all kind of assumptions, make all kind of assumptions and then link that to Markale where nothing of the kind has been, as far as I'm -- as far as I understand, has been established. So therefore if it is a general question, then it comes close to the expert questions. If it is specific about Markale, then I have not seen or heard any of these facts or assumptions to be further explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I prefaced my question saying specifically with Markale. I don't know how much further I can direct it to be about Markale, and I asked the witness are we talking about Markale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume we are talking about Markale, and I assume we are talking about the analyses which were done by me and by my team on the 11th and 12th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So what we are then talking about is -- let's then have a look at what the team did, what they wrote down about it, and then if the finding was A, B or C, then to ask the witness further questions about that. Then we know what we are talking about. At this moment it is Markale, and it's at the same time a very general approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Rule 92 ter has been utilised for this witness to introduce his transcript and has been utilised to introduce a report on this investigation. If I must go through every step of that then I will need several days for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take us to the report. Take us to the page, and then -- then we know exactly what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- did you prepare a report with your findings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no problem that he did prepare a report. Take us to the report and to the page and then we are able to follow your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if the witness prepared a report why can't I have the witness's knowledge of the report? Why can't he testify to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you should assist us take us in taking us to the part of the report where you were questions about, where your questions are of a very general nature and you don't have to ask the witness whether he wrote a report. That is not in dispute. Just say to us, I'm focusing now on this report or on testimony page that and that. We'll be able to follow and we'll then proceed as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd love to, Your Honours, except the report that I used in preparations is not the same report that's in evidence because it was changed this morning, so I don't have the page references for Your Honours. But let us turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Weber will assist you, I take it. Exhibit number already assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 5 -- 538. P538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe to assist Mr. Ivetic if he's using the report, in the upper right corner of the documents that have been admitted there's a 2 of -- it starts at 2 of 46. That will put him in the approximate page range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We all have access to e-court. I have it already on my screen in e-court on the basis of the exhibit number. That's the document we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the page -- first of all, sir, am I correct that a number of individuals assisted or participated in the preparation of this report with --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the report, the findings were that there were six potential locations that could have been the source of the -- of the incoming round and it could not be determined what side of the confrontation line the round came from; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And from the six positions from which it was said that the incoming fire could have come from, four were on the SRK or the Bosnian Serb side and two were on the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Presidency side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to that area that we're talking about that could be the potential area that a shell could have come in from, I now return to my original question which was: From that area would it also be possible for a mobile mortar being used in a shoot and scoot capacity to have fired from those areas and to have been the source of the shell that impacted on the Markale marketplace in February of 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to -- I'd like to ask you in regards to Markale. Were you able to perform a traditional fuse tunnel test to determine the bearing or direction of the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, but it -- the ground had been somewhat disturbed so it wasn't as accurate as I would have liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we get back to your report, I'd like to ask you about something that you had -- in one of your prior written statements. If I can return to 1D441, and first if we could have the first page so the witness could recognise the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ivetic, did you say 441 or 411?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 441, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, we now have the first page up on the screen and it has some signatures on the bottom, if you could focus on those. Does this appear to be one of your prior statements dated December 13, 14, 15 of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it signed by you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could turn to the sixth page in court in English and the seventh page in B/C/S and I'd like to focus on the last paragraph in the English that leads on to the next page, and on the B/C/S it's all on the same page. And I'd like to present you with what you affirmed in your statement on that day and then I'll ask you for some comments on it. First of all: "I later spoke with Colonel Radislav Cvetkovic, commander of the BSA artillery to the eastern side of Sarajevo who denied that they had fired the shell and who stated that he had fired 30- to 40.000 on the city in the previous year, so why would he deny this one if it was not true?" First of all, sir, having now seen and having heard me read this selection of your statement, do you agree that this is in relation to the Markale investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that this section of the statement that I read to you is truthful and accurate as to your knowledge and recollection of this discussion that you had with -- or encounter with Colonel Cvetkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to be clear so there is no confusion, Colonel Cvetkovic's statement to you has to be understood as denying that the BSA fired that shell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this 1995 statement that you -- that contains this testimony from you was taken just over one year after you had the meeting with Colonel Cvetkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Slightly more. I had the meeting with Colonel Cvetkovic on the 14th, I think, of February, 1994, and the statement, as you pointed out, was taken around the 11th to the 12th of December, 1995, but I remember to this day very clearly the conversation I had with Colonel Cvetkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does the selection we've just read from your 1995 statement comport with your very clear recollections?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's all I needed, sir. Thank you. Now, as part of your investigation into the Markale incident, did you become aware that there was a police building or headquarters within 300 metres of the site of the blast?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to return to P538, and I believe it should be page 54 in the e-court of the version that is in e-court. And while we wait for that, sir, the report that is on the screen is -- is part of the packet that is the result of your investigative team's efforts and -- and am I correct that this is the prior investigative team -- Mr. Captain Verdy, this is his findings or his cover sheet of his report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that this was available to you and indeed reviewed by you prior to making your own conclusions as to the bearing of the shell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I'm not sure as to whether I reviewed it before or after I conducted my own investigation but it was certainly made available at that time, and I found it, as I'm sure you're about to introduce, as being completely and utterly wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First I'd like to focus on the item labelled as G, description of evidence. Description -- pardon me, description of damage. And there it states: "The mortar shell impacted on the wood of a stall (0.9 metres from the ground) so that the analysis was very difficult." Do you agree with this assessment by Captain Verdy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the shell impacted at ground level or some distance above ground level?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I believe that the shell impacted on the ground and detonated either at ground level or slightly below ground level, very slightly below.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that by the time you arrived at the site much of the location had been swept and most of the debris had been removed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I would say that a lot of debris had been removed but sufficient remained that we could conduct a proper analysis of the situation and the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please turn to page 51 in e-court of this same document in the English and page 70 in the B/C/S version. And Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill this is what is identified as an amplification of the analysis, and it's signed on the next page by Major John Russell. First of all, who was Major Russell in relation to the investigative team that you partook?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Major Russell was not a member of the investigative team. He was, I believe, the military advisor or military assistant to the commander of the UN force in Bosnia. I didn't meet him. I didn't meet him specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can focus on the part labelled part with the number 1. This which we can -- you can read. It's on the bottom of the screen. This section indicates that a minimum of three craters is necessary to give a better chance of confirming a weapons system location. Would you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It certainly would help, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, now talking about the Markale incident, there was only crater, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at his description which is also contained in part 1 where he states: "In this situation, the mortar round apparently struck vendor's table which initiated the round just prior to striking the ground. This can be confirmed by, one, the small crater's signature (a 120-millimetre mortar would naturally make a bigger crater on the pavement found at the market) and, two, the amount of casualties generated by the explosion leads one to conclude that a slightly above-ground explosion occurred." Do you -- did you and your team agree with this assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you or other members of your team have an opportunity to dispute or discuss these findings with other UN personnel involved?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The team discussed them with the team. There was a total of four members on the team plus two technical advisors, and we discussed it amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just so that we're clear, how many members of the team were there in addition to yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Team leader, three members, myself, and an EOD expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it the unanimous conclusion of all team members that the precise source of the fire could not be distinguished; that is, that either side could have been the source for this shell, either the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to now move to the Dobrinja investigation and specifically deal with that particular investigation that you were [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move on, could I ask the witness one or two questions. Mr. Hamill, have you read any of the reports which were later produced before this Tribunal by experts Vilicic and Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you in any other way familiarised yourselves with what in addition to the technical possibilities you had at the time were available to experts that later studied and examined the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. When we concluded our report on the 15th of February, that was the end of it, as far as we were concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now again so we're clear, Colonel - I apologise for having to repeat this - but so that everybody's clear now let's talk about Dobrinja. First of all, the two craters that you found on site were filled with a red substance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any documents you're referring to or just the testimony of the witness in the previous case; and if so, what page approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's call up Exhibit 1D435.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has not received an exhibit number yet, Mr. -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No. This is 65 ter number 1D435.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which I believe is an information sheet dated the 18th of September, 2011, and is the result of a meeting between Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill and members of the Prosecution, specifically Mr. Barry Hogan and Mr. Chester Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, do you recall a meeting with the Prosecution on the date in question?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention to the third paragraph on this document. It says and I begin: "The craters are old, and both have been filled with a red substance that has the effect of largely preserving them. However, the process did interfere with the craters to some extent. I made the assumption that the craters were not interfered with unduly, and that the red substance was the only interference. Crater 1, the easternmost, was better preserved than crater 2. The interference was such that it is not possible at this time to determine whether the craters were made by a gun or a mortar. However, there were indications in crater 1 that it was a light-calibre gun. There were traces of 'wings' which are characteristic of a crater formed by a shell from a gun or howitzer, rather than a mortar bomb. That is not to say that it was definitely not a mortar. If it was, it was most likely a medium mortar. I made examinations based on both types of projectiles, using different methods. Given the condition of the craters, the results were not significantly different." First of all, sir, my reading of this, are these your words?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do they accurately and truthfully depict your observations as you remember them as to these two craters in the Dobrinja region?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did anyone ever advise you who had placed the red substance in these craters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Possibly I was told at the time that it was done by the authorities, but I cannot say at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever experienced the use of such a substance in prior crater analyses that you've performed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge and in your military training, is the use of any such substance ever been presented as an accepted practice for the investigation of craters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. But the reason for the plasticisation, if you can call it that, was to preserve the craters in their original state or as close to their original state as a memory to those who were killed at that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The red substance, I presume, prevented the fuse tunnel method from being employed by you to determine the direction or bearing of the shot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think we've now twice made reference to the fuse tunnel method. I know it's in your transcript, but could you please briefly describe for us how that fuse tunnel method is employed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Okay. What happens is that when a mortar bomb hits the ground, it impacts at a particular angle. The fuse is at the top. The fuse is largely undamaged and is driven forward by the force of the explosion. This causes a tunnel several centimetres in length at a specific angle. Following on from that, the tail fin of the mortar which is inert, in other words, it does not have explosive substances attached, continues and follows the fuse down the fuse tunnel. So we have a very good normal angle of incidence of the mortar bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the bottom of this document that is in e-court before us, your information sheet from proofing with the Prosecution, I see here that you state that it is your professional opinion that the rounds that impacted on Dobrinja on 01 June 1993 came from the L5A position and were most likely a 122-millimetre projectile. Is this accurate as to your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is accurate, but as I stated there, that is an opinion. I am not stating it as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. And is that because you cannot 100 per cent exclude the possibility the -- both were caused by a mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
