utterances.text: And I have another question. Is it also possible that it could have been an 82-millimetre shell that could cause at least one of the craters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And your opinion that the L5A site could be a source for the fire, would that be due to it being a known artillery position in the general bearing that you determined?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And it was one which I had personal knowledge of at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As you sit here today, you cannot exclude the possibility that there are unknown sites in that same general bearing including mobile shoot and scoot units?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: There were definitely mortar units based in the same area. That's a fact. And they weren't employed in shoot and scoot area. They were located permanently in the Toplik area. So it could have been fired from those. It's within range.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Just waiting for the transcript to catch up.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As to the location where the shells fell, you conducted your investigation several years after the conclusion of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you cannot speak as to any military instalments or structures that may have been in that general area when the shots actually fell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, and I have to emphasise it is to the best of my knowledge, because we had UNMOs in that area on a daily basis there were no military targets there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned the gun position L5A. I presume that would be Lima 5A.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was that gun position monitored by the UNMO mission at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen or heard of a shoot-rep report from that particular location that matched with the date and time and type of ordinance as to the shot that fell on Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not to my memory. Could I say that it was several years afterwards when I was approached in terms of the Dobrinja incident, and I would have not had information recorded with me at that time. It is possible, due to the position I was in, that I did receive a report at the time, but if so, as I say, it's long gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I presume that any such report would not have been the basis of your conclusion or opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In regard to being approached in terms of the Dobrinja incident, could you detail for us who approached you to examine the Dobrinja incident years after the incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I was approached by the ICTY OTP, I presume, Mr. Chester Stamp and Mr. Barry Hogan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could witness and counsel please make pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were you engaged in the capacity of an expert for purposes of that examination?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say the OTP, you mentioned two individuals. Am I correct they're the same individuals that are named on this information sheet?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to some other areas of your personal involvement or knowledge, so I'd like to go back to the time when you were an UNMO in Sarajevo, and I'd like to look again at your 1995 statement. So that's 65 ter number 1D441. And this time, page 4 of the same in the English and page 4 also in the B/C/S. And, sir, I'd ask for us to focus on the third paragraph from the top, and that reads as follows: "My experience was that before the Serbs fired their artillery, they called in the team members, they made their elevation, bearing and waited for UNMOs before they fired the guns. This was my experience on the south side of the city." First off, Colonel, can you confirm the truthfulness and accuracy of this part of the statement, your 1995 statement that I have just read?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. That was certainly the case for most of the firings from Lima 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've anticipated my question by going specifically to Lima 5. Is it meant to be Lima 5 or is this, generally speaking, true for all of the Lima sites that you had knowledge of on the south side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Lima 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to turn to 65 ter 1D439, which is a transcript of some of the testimony that you gave in 2010 in the Karadzic proceedings. I will be looking for page 62 in e-court, beginning on line 1. That should correlate to transcript page 9734 of that case's record of transcript. And again the first several lines of the page are what I'd like to focus on, so if we can zoom in on that for the benefit of everyone who's following. And I will read for you, sir, and you can follow along: "Q. In contrast to the Serb, as you confirmed through your observations, the Muslim Army often changed their positions. They had mortars either on trucks or they changed their positions, as such. You observed that the Serbs mostly had stationary weapons. They did not move them; right? "A. In general times -- in general terms, the VRS did not move their heavy weapons. They kept them in situ, which made it very easy to keep an eye on them." First of all, Colonel, can you confirm the accuracy of this selection of the Karadzic testimony, that it comports to your knowledge and recollections.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is accurate insofar as it goes. However, we were not aware of all artillery positions of the VRS on the south side and particularly not on the north side of the city. We were told at one stage by a VRS commander that we only knew about 12 per cent of their weapons. I think he was exaggerating downward.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on the other side, the Muslim side. Am I correct that the weapons during the time period that you were there on the Muslim side were not all being easily tracked by the UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I presume when you say the Muslim side, you mean the Armija BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Papa side [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Or Papa side. Yes, I can accept that. They were not easily tracked, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can continue reading from this same page, line numbers 9 through 14. And again, sir, I'll present you with the question and answer and ask for some follow-up. The question was: "Q. Thank you. In the southern part of Sarajevo, you saw Serb artillery positions. When the Serbs wanted to fire their mortars or use their other artillery pieces, they informed the monitors of their intention, they would mention what their targets would be, and they asked whether the monitors wanted to observe that; right? "A. That certainly happened on many occasions." Does that comport with your experience and recollection of that experience?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when it was presented to you that the Serb artillery units that you were observing and dealt with would tell UNMOs their targets that they were shooting at, is that something that you have personal knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is something that I am aware of, but you must remember that the UNMOs were a very mixed background. We had army, navy, and air force, very many of whom would have no experience with artillery weapons and would not be able to technically examine the end product, as it were, of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But you do not dispute that the Serb artillery operators would advise them of what the target was before shooting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That would generally be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek clarification. When you say that would generally be the case, generally be the case on the many occasions where that happened? Is that, I have to understand, generally being the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The VRS personnel that you interacted with, the actual artillery commanders or operators, did they seem co-operative and forthcoming with you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and would you say that you established a good relationship with many VRS members during the time you were there as an UNMO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the vast majority of people that you met on the VRS side were locals; that is to say, that they were persons who lived in the local area surrounding Sarajevo or had come from the centre of Sarajevo as refugees, that they were local -- local to that terrain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: As IDPs, not as refugees. They were within their own country. But yes to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. The area of the Lukavica barracks where you spent much of your time when you were an UNMO, did it receive fairly regular fire from the Bosnian Presidency side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It received fire on irregular occasions from the Presidency side, yes. Both small arms and mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn back to your statement of 1995, 1D441, and this time it will be page 4 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, and it will be the second paragraph from the top in the English which reads as follows: "On 26 May 1993, there was a civilian area in the BSA-held territory attacked by ABiH with 82-millimetre mortars. The rounds began to come in in Vojkovici at 1058. The ABiH fired in total 13 rounds plus infantry fire. The response from the BSA came at 1140. They fired ten shells. The incoming rounds came from -- came in from Hrasnica-Igman area." Does this paragraph of your 1995 statement comport truthfully and accurately with your recollections and knowledge of this incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall that there had been an agreement reached between the warring parties that a portion of the territory at the Hrasnica-Igman area had been given to the UN and vacated by the Serbs which the army of BiH then, in violation of the agreement, took over from the UN?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I do recall that, but it was not at that time. That was approximately towards the end of July. It wasn't in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up for me. That's --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return to 1D439, and page 73 in e-court and focus on line 22 of the same. It's again the transcript of the proceedings from the Karadzic case, and it should be -- I apologise. Is this page 70 of the ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is page 73 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It should be page 70. Sorry. And again, it should be the lines 22 and further. Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Starting with the question and it will tell you the time-frame I'm talking about, sir: "Q. On the 5th of December, 1993, you went to Kiseljak to attend a conference, and then you moved to the Papa side. You saw the Kosevo Hospital, and you saw two nurses and one doctor killed by a shell. You also saw a hole in a wall over 1 metre in diameter, forming almost a perfect circle. Do you remember that? "A. That is almost correct. I didn't see any nurses or a doctor killed. I was informed, when we were there, that there had been those casualties when the building was hit by a shell, but that had happened some time before and I don't know when. I did see the hole in the wall. It was a large one, and it was almost a perfect circle. So, yes, that part is correct." First of all, when you're talking -- does this comport with your recollection, your factual observations at the Kosevo Hospital building in December of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, my answer does. The question obviously doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that you reached a conclusion based upon this factual observation as to the fire more likely having coming from inside the Muslim or Papa zone rather than from the VRS as is, I believe, contained in the next four lines of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That was my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd ask you to give us a little bit of a -- briefly the factual backdrop or bases for that opinion you have. Explain the same.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Okay. It seemed to me that the fire was a very flat trajectory. It doesn't come in at an angle otherwise the shape of the hole would have been different. But it looked as if it was almost a flat trajectory. So it hit and it exploded, and when I looked to the north from where the round had to have been fired I was only looking within the Presidency area. It was not possible to see ground or territory held by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you said it had a very flat trajectory, would that -- it seemed to indicate an artillery weapon in a direct fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That would indicate a round that was fired either directly by an artillery weapon or alternately by a tank. It would have been fired at a very high velocity, so it was very possibly a tank round.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look -- scroll further down on this page at lines 20 to 23. Here you are talking about one shelling incident involving Kosevo Hospital that looked like it originated from a Muslim army tank positioned north of the hospital, and your answer was: "That was my conclusion, yes." Is this the same incident or a different incident that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That was the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in e-court of the document that is up on the screen. That should be transcript page 9744 of the Karadzic proceedings. And if we could focus for a moment on line 9 of the same, and I'd like to present again the question and answer for you and ask for you to provide more details: "Q. Do you agree that it was your view that the Muslim side, or Bosnian side, if you wish, took political advantage of incidents and that these incidents frequently occurred at the same time as various international conferences were convened? "A. That was certainly my view, my opinion, yes. But it was my personal opinion, as such, not a UN position." Does this part of the transcript from the Karadzic case truthfully and accurately depict your -- your opinion, I guess, is -- your personal opinion as presented by you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you have just read out my answer. I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the information report from your proofing session with the Office of the Prosecutor earlier this year, you mentioned an incident that had been reported to you of some Serb villages that had been attacked by the Armija near Han Pijesak. Do you recall the date or any other reference you can give for those reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That -- yes. That would have been probably around June, the end of May, June, and into July in 1993, when we were informed by the liaison team in the VRS HQ in Lukavica that villages had been attacked, burned, civilians killed, Serbian -- Serb villagers, Serb villages, and they had been attacked by the Armija. So we requested through the liaison office that we should go and visit those villages to verify what had happened and we were refused permission. We requested on a number of occasions when these incidents were reported to us that we should investigate and it was consistently refused. So we informed our interlocutors that due to their refusal, we would not report the incidents because we did not have first-hand knowledge of such incidents, and we had no eyewitness reports from an independent source.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are you familiar with Francis Roy Thomas who was the SMO in Sarajevo from October 1993 to July 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge that Mr. Thomas went to an area near Han Pijesak and investigated a village that had been attacked in this -- in a similar manner?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: As I mentioned, I was discussing the period from May until July. Roy Thomas arrived in October, as you said. So, no, I would have no personal knowledge. At that time I was working in the headquarters as deputy chief operations officer, and we had reports in from throughout Croatia, Bosnia, Macedonia, and Serbia in relation to incidents occurring here, there, and everywhere. So one particular village and incident wouldn't really stick out in my mind. I was dealing with the whole of the former Yugoslavia with the exception of Slovenia at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We do have a report where the SMO, Mr. Thomas, is identifying various villages that according to some NATO intelligence had showed a similar pattern of destruction. Do you recall the names of any of the villages that you personally heard of such that that would be able to refresh your recollection or -- can I have the answer verbally, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't help you, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'd like to move to -- I'd like to get some clarification, if I can, from you relative to some features related to the aiming and shooting of artillery. First of all, could you tell us how many years you've been an artillery officer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I served in the artillery corps since May 1970. I've been an officer since 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have talked about mortars in this case being -- or in terms of the accuracy of mortars. With respect to mortars, am I correct that their tube is not -- is ungrooved, is smooth?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Some mortars are rifled and some are unrifled. The majority of mortars would be unrifled which would make them more inherently inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could focus on mortars, and am I correct that in terms of mortars one uses a term to describe their landing point as the "beaten" zone?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I also correct that this is an elliptical pattern of a certain area where a number of shells fired from the same piece with the same aim sightings might land?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you give us a more detailed description of the concept of a beaten zone as to the number of shells that might be expected to land in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In general terms, 50 per cent of the bombs fired from a mortar at a specific bearing angle and charge would land within the beaten zone. Another 50 per cent would land outside that. But you can take it that the beaten zone is quite large and depends on a number of factors including atmospheric conditions, charge temperature, air pressure and the charge it's fired at, the distance, the angle of elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I have most of those. I'd like to ask you about one that you did not include -- or maybe did not include, if I'm reading correctly. Am I correct it also depends on the type of shell that is being used?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Well, we were talking about shells being the same type, I thought. High explosive shells of a particular nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The beaten zone --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- as it were, the area of that elliptical -- the size of that elliptical area will vary depending on the type of shell that is at issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It will vary depending on the type of shell, but generally smoke ammunition and high-explosive ammunition has the same ballistic characteristics, so it wouldn't vary that much. It varies with the individual shells themselves. Because of the fact that mortar bombs are not made to the same tolerances that are artillery shells are made, there are slight discrepancies between them. Maybe just a gram or two grams of weight which would make a deference. Equally, the charge temperature might be slightly different than one and the next, which would impact on the speed at which the explosion occurs that drives the bomb forward in the barrel. Equally, the bomb having been fired goes through various different atmospheric layers, and there will be changes in the wind speed and direction in each of those layers even from moment to moment. These are some of the factors which impact on where the bomb will actually land. And bear in mind that for a 120-millimetre bomb, the lethal radius is 54 metres, and the danger zone for unprotected troops is 500 metres radius. For protected troops, in other words troops who are in trenches, for example, it's still 250 metres radius, which means that within 250 metres radius of the detonation of a 120-millimetre mortar bomb, it is possible to be injured. It is not necessarily the case that one would be injured, but it is certainly within the bounds of possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've used a term that I'm familiar with, lethal radius. Could you please explain the concepts of lethal radius and danger radius to the members of the panel.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The lethal radius is one in which one may expect to be killed by an explosion of a mortar bomb within that distance. As I say, it isn't always the case that one dies. One may even escape injury, such being the flukes of ballistics. But generally one can expect to be killed if one is unprotected within 54 metres of a 120-millimetre mortar bomb. The danger area is where the shrapnel continues at such a speed that it will injure somebody who is unprotect, and that, as I said, for a 120-bomb normally is considered to be 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock. Would this be a suitable moment or could you find a suitable moment in the next two or three minutes to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This would be a suitable moment before I move on to more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could I also ask you whether despite the short delay you are still on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are. Then we take a break, but not until after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Ivetic, it wouldn't be of great use to take another break. Therefore, the Chamber is considering that we should continue exceptionally for 75 minutes and adjourn at -- without any further breaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you spent some time discussing the beaten zone, the lethal radius and the danger radius of shells. Would I then be correct in concluding from this that in order to be considered militarily on target a round doesn't have to strike that target dead on but merely needs to get within one of these zones or radiuses to be able to neutralise that target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In artillery terms it depends on the type of mission whether it's neutralising or destruction. A destruction mission is one which targets very specifically a point or points in order to destroy it. It's very time consuming to get on target, and it's very heavy on ammunition. What the normal use for artillery is to neutralise a target; in other words, to prevent the target from reacting or from acting. So this would mean that when the round reached the general area of the target, it would be considered to be a target round. If it's within 25, 50 metres, it's certainly considered to be on target.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again depending on the target, if it is within the lethal or danger radius, that could also be sufficient to neutralise a particular target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, because we're talking in terms of around 30 to 50 metres depending on the type of shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to go through some of the factors that you, I believe, mentioned a few questions ago that affect the accuracy of a shell. And I'd like to go through them step-by-step to try and make sure it's clear for everyone, even for those of us that are laypersons. The first variable, I believe, is of a purely mechanical nature, the actual ordnance itself. I would first like to ask you about so-called tube like. Is it correct that the more rounds that have been shot through the tube the less accurate the piece becomes even if rifled?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The next variable I would like to discuss is the quality of the explosive propellant actually used. Am I correct that with uneven burning characteristics the trajectory of an expelled shell can also be affected?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now for this question focus on the investigation into the Markale incident. And as far as the propellant is concerned, when your team visited both the VRS and the Armija BiH sites, you saw ordnance at both locations that appeared to be not factory made. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, it is not accurate. The team did not visit any sites. There was a visit by members of Sector Sarajevo under Colonel Pardon, who visited the BiH sites, the Army of BiH sites, in 105 Brigade and I think 2 Mountain Brigade, but our team did not. There was no requirement to so do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you know, did those visits result in viewing ordnance that was not factory made?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I understand that Colonel Pardon from his report reported that he had seen ammunition which was not factory made, or at least not conventional munition factory made. It was clearly made in some type of a factory or workshop but it was not from a conventional military source. But that's hearsay, by the way, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's contained in the document that's been entered into evidence as P583 [sic]. I'd like to ask about meteorological variables. Am I correct that in order to more accurately fire an artillery round one needs to know the air temperature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that generally speaking the hotter the air, the greater range of a round, whereas the colder the air and denser the air the fall of shot is steeper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That would be generally correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can focus for a moment on your investigation related to Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question in relation to this. Could you give us an indication as to, well, let's say a difference of 5 Celsius decrease. What difference would that make on a shell which would, well, let's say, travel on average 2.5 kilometres? Would it then be 2.6 or 2.4, or would it be 3 or 4? I mean, what's the, more or less, the margin of -- well, I wouldn't say error, but the margin of difference for a degree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be a matter of some metres, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's all. It would be very minor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are talking about 2.5 kilometres or 2.510 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More or less. Yes, I'm not debating on 5 or 10 more metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But to get an impression. That would, therefore, then be, well, let's say, less than -- certainly less than half a per cent. Half a per cent would be 12.5 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In terms -- in terms of charge temperature alone that would probably be correct, sir, but it's a combination of not just the charge temperature and the air temperature, but also the wind speed, the wind direction and various other factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and if you would add that up that would then lead to perhaps 50, 100 metres, and -- yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And also, Mr. President, it would depend on the type of shell, so that, for example, a mortar bomb would be more affected by these factors than an artillery shell because it would be going through more layers of air at a much slower speed so it would be -- it would be much more affected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us an indication of what that effect would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be 100 metres in any direction at a distance of, say, 3.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And we are still talking in terms of a small percentage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could focus on the examination -- or the incident in Dobrinja. Am I correct that the air temperature and/or the barometric pressure were not factors that you had available to you from that day when the shell was fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Clearly not, but they were totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With -- you've mentioned, I believe, wind loft. Okay. With regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you would allow me again one question to clarify. We -- I do understand that tables are made, that fired on this angle a projectile will travel at such a distance. Is there a kind of a standard measurement that you say this is the standard for our tables is 20 degrees Celsius, wind less than so-and-so, much tail-wind or no wind at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that no wind at all? Temperature is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Temperature would be standard, so I think probably 15 or 20 degrees [overlapping speakers] I'm not sure to be honest. But it would be entered at the beginning of the firing tables what the standard conditions are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so they are known.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Another variable that needs to be taken into account for the accuracy of any outgoing round would also be the actual maps that were being used by the artillery commander to direct the fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite put it like that. The map is important in order to get in the general area of the target, but after that, one adjusts the round onto the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what in -- in the military term adjustment rounds is used, are those actually regular mortar shells just fired at a bearing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, they are. What happens with a normal artillery shoot, shall we say, is that an observer chooses a target. He informs the gun position of the co-ordinates of the target and his direction to the target. At that stage, one round is fired at the target. This comes up either on target or much more likely it comes up somewhere off target, and the observer then corrects it in relation to his position. So he will tell the gun position that it's right or left or it's up or down. So he's looking for them to add or drop or to go left or right. And they do that with their next round, and that's closer, hopefully, and then perhaps a further fourth round is actually a target round, and then they go into what's called fire for effect, where you might fire five rounds from six weapons at the target. That would be standard artillery conventional warfare practice, but clearly it was not something which happened to a great extent in the Sarajevo area during 1993, 1994, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one other clarifying question, Mr. Ivetic. One of the previous questions was whether the accuracy of the outgoing rounds would also be influenced by the actual maps that were being used. Now, I have some difficulties in understanding the question, and therefore I think you also did not exactly address the question, unless I misunderstood it. If you use an incorrect map, I take it that you make the wrong calculations as how to fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends, Mr. President, on the type of equipment that the observer is using. It may be that he is using a laser range finder, for example, which will give him an exact position of the location, or he may be just using the bare map, in which case he would probably not be more accurate than within 100 by 100 metres. If you remember, we were talking about grid references earlier on. He would normally give down a six-figure grid which means 100 by 100. If the map was inherently inaccurate or his equipment was wrongly calibrated then clearly there would be an issue of the target not being as close to -- or the round not being as close to the target as it should be first -- even first time round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what triggered you to answer that by adjusting the next round would resolve that problem if any inaccuracies would result --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from that combination of two factors: Equipment and the details of the maps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, the single rounds that would have been fired as adjustment rounds, those would still be, I presume, lethal rounds with the same lethal radius and danger zone as the target round?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, they would have exactly the same characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Occasionally in areas of difficult visibility it might be that one would use a smoke round, and you might remember earlier on there was a reference to gas. My opinion was that that would have been a smoke round which was fired in an area of difficult visibility, because it isn't always possible to see the fall of shot where the round comes down, so smoke could be used to get a better indication of where the round comes down. But ballistically the smoke round and the high explosive round would have the same ballistic characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to ask you if you can estimate for us how many analyses of craters you have performed to determine the bearing of the incoming fire in your career?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not very many. I couldn't give you any sort of a number as such, but it wouldn't be more than a few dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it part of your formal training to deal with craters and determine the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I've been doing it since 1978 in Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you perform instruction in the military as to this skill?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I spent three years in the artillery school in our defence forces teaching this amongst other subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I just also seek just for my understanding, bearing means just ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Direction. Direction, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Direction only exclusively, no distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is -- is keeping abreast of all developments and new techniques or studies in mortar crater analysis, was it part of your job when you were an instructor at the artillery school defence forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it was, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just check one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill, I thank you for your time and your testimony today. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: A few if I could, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill, did you find any evidence that the mortar that hit the Markale market came from a mobile mortar on the Presidency side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does the location that a mobile mortar, you were asked about the shoot and scoot method, that that mobile mortar is fired from remain a target after the mobile mortar has left that location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It should not so do, but I'm not saying at any stage that there was a mobile mortar fired at at this time or that there was one anywhere in the area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Maybe this would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, for the accuracy of the transcript, is my recollection right that you asked one of the previous questions whether Mr. Hamill did find any evidence that the mortar that hit the Markale market came from a round fired from the Presidency side because now it reads did you find that the mortar and I think you were asking about evidence about it being fired from the Presidency side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For clarity, if I can repeat the question and just seek the confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The question that I thought I read in was -- which appears to be a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Different perhaps from and it may be relevant. If you would repeat your question and then we'd see whether Mr. Hamill gives the same or a different answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you find any evidence that the mortar that hit the Markale market came from a mobile mortar on the Presidency side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Same answer: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could return or maybe more clearly ask you the question. If a mortar is firing from a location, in returning fire is the target the mortar or the location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The target has to be the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So is there any type of confirmation that you would seek before returning fire on a mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Well, I would expect it would be in the same position until such time as I found different. With modern equipment, it's possible to locate a mortar very quickly and get information to a counter-battery gun to fire on that position. Mortars are inherently dangerous places to be around in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, has the questions in re-examination triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Further cross-examination by Mr. Ivetic:

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If a mobile mortar had been the source of fire for the Markale incident, would you expect to find any physical evidence of the same with the type of examination that your team performed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not at Markale, it wouldn't be possible. It doesn't matter where the round was fired from or in what capacity the weapon was located. The end result is that a mortar bomb hit the market place in Markale at a particular angle, at a particular time, on a particular day, and caused certain damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Upon further considering I have one question for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with or do you have specific knowledge about the analysis of a mortar impact on the basis also of the speed of the projectile upon impact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The higher the speed on impact the further down the tunnel will go, but also at a particular time, the mortar bomb reaches a terminal velocity which is limited by the fact that it's moving through air which is causing some resistance. Everything falling accelerates at a particular rate and then ceases to accelerate because of air resistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I was hinting at knowledge which would allow on the basis of the speed of impact to make further findings on the trajectory of the projectile and the distance the projectile travelled.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I am not aware of any literature, sir, that provides that sort of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. This was one more question, Mr. Ivetic. If that triggered any further questions, then of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Hamill, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, for having answered all the questions that were put to you, and -- both questions by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am addressing the parties. I do not know exactly what you agreed upon as far as scheduling is concerned. I think there was a request for the next witness to start his examination on Thursday morning as a result of a long travel, and that in that case then the parties would have agreed that the evidence of that witness will be received in its entirety tomorrow without additional sessions. Is that still the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. We intend to stay within our estimate. It's my understanding that that would, with the cross, still conclude tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is a commitment by the parties they have agreed upon, and we will then start tomorrow with the evidence of that witness and not today. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few procedural matters which we could deal with at this very moment, but if there's anything, Mr. Weber, you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you don't mind I'll put one quick thing on the record just so we're able to later associate it. During the cross-examination, reference was made to 1D435. I just wanted to put on the record that this is the same document that's referred to in the witness's previous testimony that's been admitted at pages 6114 to 6117. I believe otherwise it would be kind of hard to associate the current testimony and the previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Reference was made to it. It was not tendered do you wish to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could tender it at this moment if it would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 1D435 would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D104, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D104 is admitted into evidence. Then a few matters. First - and it deals with the MFI'd exhibits P517 up to and including P520 and P522 - the Chamber has considered the objections that were raised against the admission of the exhibits that were marked for identification Friday the 16th of November, 2012, during the testimony of Witness Birte Weiss and now admits into evidence Exhibits P517, P518, P519, P520, and P522. There is another matter. When we discussed recently a Rule 70 motion -- and perhaps I better go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We dealt with the matter which should have been in private session. We also dealt with one correction on the transcript and a time limit to respond to a translation matter which we could have dealt with in open session. We adjourn for the day. We resume tomorrow, Thursday the 22nd of November at 9.30 in this same Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of November, 2012, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
